articles.headline_en: Italian far-right leader criticised after using AI to digitally undress female MP
articles.significance: The incident illustrates how politically connected public figures can use manipulated imagery on social media and trigger platform-moderation and public-accountability concerns.
articles.summary_en: Roberto Vannacci, founder of Italy’s Futuro Nazionale party, shared an AI-manipulated image of Forza Italia MP Matilde Siracusano on Facebook. The altered image removed clothing from the original photograph, prompting accusations of sexism and offensive conduct; reports say Vannacci claimed he had reposted the image rather than created it.

articles.headline_en: Jordan Bardella denies report that he made antisemitic remarks
articles.significance: The case concerns alleged political speech in private digital messages and the public use of social media to contest their authenticity and political consequences.
articles.summary_en: France 24 reported that Jordan Bardella, leader of France’s National Rally, denied allegations by investigative outlet Mediapart that he had written antisemitic comments in private chats in 2013, when he was 17 or 18. Bardella rejected the allegations on X, describing them as fabricated.

articles.headline_en: Police question 27 people over election-day social-media posts
articles.significance: Cyprus is enforcing a statutory blackout on election-related online content, including unpaid personal posts, raising questions about the scope of restrictions on political expression.
articles.summary_en: Cypriot police began questioning 27 people over more than 100 social-media posts and advertisements allegedly linked to parliamentary elections and published during the legally prohibited period before or on polling day. The investigation followed 127 complaints, and authorities said the law applies to both paid and unpaid election-related content, including posts by ordinary citizens.

articles.headline_en: Police investigate 27 people over potentially illegal election posts
articles.significance: The investigation demonstrates how election regulations can criminalise online political communication beyond candidates and official campaign material.
articles.summary_en: Authorities are examining more than 100 social-media posts after complaints about possible breaches of Cyprus’s election blackout rules. The law prohibits election-related posts, news and advertisements during the restricted period and allows for imprisonment, a fine, or both; one person under investigation said she had posted as a private citizen.

articles.headline_en: Italian foreign minister’s altered images go viral
articles.significance: The episode highlights the circulation of manipulated political imagery online and the reputational effects of viral content involving public officials.
articles.summary_en: Euronews reported on viral images depicting Italy’s Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani in a miniskirt. Tajani apologised and said he had not intended to offend women; the available report does not establish whether the images were removed or identify a formal moderation action.

editorial_overview: The articles show several forms of conflict over political speech online: manipulated images targeting public figures, disputed historical messages, and legal restrictions on election-related posts. Cyprus provides the clearest example of state enforcement, with police investigating both paid campaign material and unpaid personal posts during an election blackout. In France and Italy, the disputes centre more on the political consequences of alleged or manipulated digital content than on formal removal orders. The available reporting does not establish a broad, coordinated European trend of government-directed takedowns during the period reviewed.
topic: European press review: political speech, content removal and social-media moderation
